CHAPTER 1 · UNIT 1 · 4 HOURS
    Introduction to Version Control

    Why version control exists, the three kinds of VCS, and setting up Git and GitHub on Windows.

      Local, centralized & distributed VCS  Benefits of Git & GitHub    Installing Git on Windows

      git config   git help    Creating a GitHub account

    Practise online: missions M-01, M-02

The Amroli Canteen problem

Meet four BCA final-year students at SBCCAS. For their project they are building Amroli
Canteen, a web app that lets students order samosas and chai before the lunch break,
so nobody waits in the queue.

  Student            Builds

  Krish              the menu and cart pages

  Dhruvi             the order system in Python

  Meet               the database

  Hetvi              team lead: plans, reviews and writes the README

In the first two weeks they share code the way many students do: WhatsApp, pen
drives and email. Here is what happened.

1 · Lost work                         2 · File-name chaos                  3 · Overwritten work
  Krish's login page worked              menu.html   ,  menu_v2.html    ,    Dhruvi and Krish both
  on Monday. On Tuesday he               menu_FINAL.html     ,               edited   app.py   and sent it
  "improved" it and broke it.            menu_FINAL_use_this.html       …    on WhatsApp. Whoever
  Monday's version is gone.                                                  sent last "won".

With Git                              With Git                             With Git
  Every commit is a saved               One file name. History keeps         Changes are merged. If
  snapshot. Krish can go                every version, with a message        two people edit the same
  back to Monday's version              saying what changed.                 line, Git stops and asks a
  in one command.                                                            human to decide.

4 · Who broke it?                     5 · No backup
  The total price shows ₹0.             Meet's laptop crashed a
  Nobody knows when it                  week before the review.
  broke or why.                         His database work was
                                        only on that laptop.

With Git                              With Git + GitHub
  The log shows who                     Every teammate and
  changed what, when and                GitHub hold a full copy. A
  why. You can find the                 crashed laptop costs
  exact change.                         minutes, not weeks.

Hetvi, the team lead, says: "Professional teams don't work like this. They use Git and
GitHub. Let's learn it properly." That is exactly what you will do in this course.

What is version control?

A version control system (VCS) is software that records changes to files over time, so
you can see who changed what and bring back any earlier version.

🧠A time machine for your project

   Think of a video game that saves your progress at every checkpoint. If you fall
   into lava, you restart from the last checkpoint instead of from the beginning. A
   VCS gives your code the same superpower, and each checkpoint is called a
   commit.

A VCS answers four questions about every change:

   What changed? (exactly which lines)

   Who changed it?

   When was it changed?

   Why? (the message the author wrote)

Three kinds of version control

Version control has grown up in three stages.

             Local VCS                       Centralized VCS                Distributed VCS  GIT

          💻 Your computer                    🖥 Central server                      ☁ GitHub
             🗄 versions                       🗄 all versions                      🗄 full copy

History lives on one                    ↕   ↕   ↕                         ↕    ↕   ↕
      machine. If its disk fails,
          history is gone.                  💻      💻      💻                💻🗄       💻🗄        💻🗄

Everyone works through one         Every computer has the full
                                          server. Server down =            history. Work offline; any
                                           nobody can commit.             copy can restore the others.

1. Local VCS. Versions are kept in a small database on one computer. An early example
is RCS (1982). Like a personal diary in your room: useful, but only you can read it, and if
the house floods it is gone.

2. Centralized VCS. One central server holds all versions. Developers check out files
from it and send changes back. Examples: CVS and Subversion (SVN). Like one library

book the whole class must share: if the library is closed, nobody can study. The server
is a single point of failure.

3. Distributed VCS. Every developer has a complete copy of the project and its whole
history on their own computer. Examples: Git and Mercurial. Like every student owning
a full photocopy of the book: if one copy is lost, any other copy can replace it.

                                 Local                    Centralized               Distributed (Git)

Where history lives            One computer             One server                Every computer

  Work offline?                  Yes                      No                        Yes

  Team work                      No                       Yes                       Yes

  If one machine dies            History lost             Everyone stuck            Nothing lost

   ✨Why Git won

Git was created in 2005 by Linus Torvalds, who also created Linux, to manage
   the Linux kernel's thousands of contributors. It is fast, works offline and makes
   branching cheap. Today almost every software company uses it.

Benefits of Git and GitHub

    Git   A TOOL                                          GitHub   A WEBSITE

              💻 Installed on your computer                                ☁ github.com

Tracks every change in a folder                       Stores Git repositories online
      Works offline                                         Needs the internet
      Free, open source (2005, Linus Torvalds)              Adds teamwork: issues, pull requests,
      Commands:      init  , add ,  commit  ,               forks
       log  …                                               Your public developer portfolio
Git works without GitHub. GitHub needs Git. Similar sites: GitLab, Bitbucket.

Git is the tool on your computer. GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories so a
team can share them. Together they give you:

   Complete history: every change, with who, when and why.

   Safe experiments: try an idea on a branch without breaking working code (Unit 3).

   Teamwork: many people work on the same project at the same time.

   Undo: go back to any earlier version in seconds (Unit 4).

   Backup: your code is safe on GitHub even if your laptop is not.

Career: your GitHub profile is a portfolio that recruiters look at.

   ⚠Git ≠ GitHub

   A common exam mistake is writing "GitHub is a version control system". Git is the
   version control system. GitHub is a hosting service built around Git. GitLab and
   Bitbucket are similar services.

Installing Git on Windows

The SBCCAS labs use Windows, so here is the Windows installer step by step. (On
macOS, Git comes with the Xcode tools; on Ubuntu, run             sudo apt install git        .)

1. Open git-scm.com and click Download for Windows. Choose the 64-bit installer.

2. Run the installer and click Next on the licence screen.

3. Select Components: keep the defaults.

4. Choosing the default editor: change Vim to Notepad or Visual Studio Code. (Vim
   confuses beginners. If it ever opens, type        :wq   and press Enter to leave.)

5. Adjusting the name of the initial branch: choose Override the default branch name
   and type    main  . GitHub uses     main   too.

6. Adjusting your PATH: keep Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party
   software (recommended).

7. SSH executable: keep Use bundled OpenSSH.

8. HTTPS transport backend: keep Use the OpenSSL library. (If the college network
   blocks GitHub, your lab admin may choose Windows Secure Channel.)

9. Line ending conversions: keep Checkout Windows-style, commit Unix-style line
    endings.

10. Terminal emulator: keep Use MinTTY.

11. Default behaviour of       git pull    : keep Fast-forward or merge.

12. Credential helper: keep Git Credential Manager. It opens a browser window to sign
    in to GitHub.

13. Keep the remaining defaults and click Install, then Finish.

 Now open Git Bash from the Start menu and check the installation:

           Git Bash

$ git --version
   git version 2.47.1.windows.1

 Your number may be newer. Any version 2.x is fine.

    💡No laptop? No problem.

    Everything in Units 1–4 can also be practised in this site's Playground, which runs
    real Git inside your browser, even on a phone.

 Telling Git who you are:            git config

 Every commit records an author name and email. Before your first commit, tell Git who
 you are. You only need to do this once per computer:

           Git Bash

$ git config --global user.name "Krish Patel"
   $ git config --global user.email "krish@example.com"

 Check your settings:

Git Bash

  $ git config --list
  init.defaultbranch=main
  user.name=Krish Patel
  user.email=krish@example.com
  $ git config user.name
  Krish Patel

  Option                          Where the setting is saved           Applies to

   --global                        ~/.gitconfig     in your home       every repository for your user
                                  folder                               account

(no option, inside a             .git/config                         only this repository
  repository)

   ⚠Use the same email as GitHub

   Use the email address you will use for your GitHub account. GitHub uses it to link
   your commits to your profile and to show the green squares on your contribution
   graph.

   📝Shared lab computers

On a shared lab PC, set your name without              --global     inside your own project
   folder, so the next student's commits are not labelled with your name.

If you forget to configure Git, your first commit stops with this message. Now you know
how to fix it:

  Author identity unknown

  *** Please tell me who you are.

  Run

git config *-global user.email "you@example.com"
    git config *-global user.name "Your Name"

Getting help:        git help

Git has its own manual built in. There are three ways to ask it for help:

  Command                      What you get

   git help                    the list of the most common Git commands

   git help <command>          the full manual page for one command, e.g.       git help commit

git <command> -h            a short summary of options, right in the terminal

          Git Bash

  $ git commit -h
  usage: git commit [-a] [-m <msg-] [--amend] [--allow-empty]

      -m <msg>     use the given message
      -a, --all    stage modified and deleted tracked files first
      --amend      replace the last commit

   💡Read the error messages

Git's messages are unusually helpful. They often tell you the exact command to
   run next. Before searching the internet, read what Git printed.

Creating your GitHub account

1. Go to github.com and click Sign up.

2. Enter your email, the same one you used in            git config     .

3. Create a strong password.

4. Choose a professional username:            krish-patel      or  krishpatel-dev       , not
    coolboy007     . It becomes your portfolio address:        github.com/krish-patel          .

5. Solve the puzzle, then type the code GitHub emails you.

6. Choose the Free plan.

7. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA): Settings → Password and authentication
   → Enable two-factor authentication. Use an authenticator app or the GitHub Mobile
   app, and save your recovery codes somewhere safe. GitHub requires 2FA for
   everyone who contributes code.

8. Add a profile photo, your name, and "BCA student at SBCCAS, Surat" in your bio.

   🧪Lab L-01: your profile README

Create a repository named exactly the same as your username (for example
    krish-patel/krish-patel         ) and tick Add a README file. Whatever you write in
   that README appears on your GitHub profile page, like a business card. The full
   steps are on the Labs page.

Unit 1 summary

   A version control system records every change: what, who, when and why.

   Local VCS keeps history on one machine; centralized VCS on one server;
   distributed VCS (Git) on every computer.

Git is the tool on your computer; GitHub is the website that hosts repositories for
   teams.

   On Windows, install Git for Windows, and set the default branch to             main   and the
   editor to Notepad or VS Code.

    git config --global user.name            and   user.email     tell Git who you are.

    git help    , git help <command>         and  git <command> -h        are your built-in
   manual.

   Create a GitHub account with a professional username and turn on 2FA.
Next, practise with Missions M-01 and M-02 below, then take the Unit 1 quiz.

CHAPTER 2 · UNIT 2 · 8 HOURS
    Getting Started with Git

    Local and remote repositories, the three stages, and the everyday commands — from your first
    commit to your first push.

      Local vs remote repositories    init · status · add · commit  push · clone    pull · fetch

      Your first repository

    Practise online: missions M-03, M-04, M-05, M-06, M-07

Your terminal survival kit

Git is used from a terminal: on Windows that is Git Bash, on a Mac the Terminal app.
You only need a handful of commands to move around:

  Command               Does                                               Example

   pwd                  print working directory: where am I?                pwd   →  /home/student

   ls                   list files (ls -a   also shows hidden               ls -a
                        ones like   .git  )

cd                   change directory (    cd ..    = up one             cd amroli-canteen
                        level,  cd ~   = home)

   mkdir                make a directory (folder)                           mkdir amroli-canteen

   touch                create an empty file                                touch notes.txt

echo "…" >           write text into a file (>>   adds to the            echo "Samosa 15" >
  file                  end)                                               menu.txt

   cat                  show a file                                         cat menu.txt

Git Bash

  $ pwd
  /home/student
  $ mkdir amroli-canteen
  $ cd amroli-canteen

   💡The number one beginner mistake

   Running Git in the wrong folder. If Git says          fatal: not a git repository             , run
    pwd    and   cd   into your project. The prompt shows your folder:             ~/amroli-
   canteen (main)       .

Local and remote repositories

A repository (or repo) is a project folder that Git tracks: your files plus their complete
history.

💻 Krish's                                        ☁ GitHub                             💻 Dhruvi's
    laptop                 git push                                      git clone        laptop
    local                                      remote repository ·                        local
                      git pull / fetch         “origin”                   git push
    repository                                                                            repository

Local repository                       Remote repository

  Lives on                your computer (the     .git            a server such as GitHub
                          folder)

  Needs internet?         No                                     Yes, to sync

  Who can see it?         only you                               your team, or the whole world if
                                                                 public

If your laptop dies     gone                                   safe

  You send work           n/a                                     git push
  with

  You get work with       n/a                                     git clone   ,  git fetch   ,  git
                                                                 pull

   🧠Your notebook and the class notice board

Your local repo is your own notebook: you can write in it anywhere, even with no
   network. The remote repo is the class notice board: everyone reads from it, and
   you pin (push) your work there when it is ready.

By convention the main remote is called           origin   .

Creating a repository:             git init

           Git Bash

  $ cd ~/amroli-canteen
  $ git init
  Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/amroli-canteen/.git/
  $ ls -a
  ./  -./  .git/

git init     creates one hidden folder,       .git   . That folder is the repository: all history,
branches and settings live inside it. Delete         .git   and the folder becomes an ordinary
folder again.

amroli-canteen/
  ├── menu.txt              ← your files (working directory)
  └── .git/                 ← the repository — Git manages this, don't edit it
       ├── HEAD              ← which branch you are on
       ├── config            ← settings for this repository
       ├── objects/          ← every saved version of every file
       ├── refs/             ← branch and tag names
       ├── hooks/            ← optional scripts
       └── info/

   ⚠Never edit .git by hand

Look inside if you are curious (       ls .git    ), but let Git manage it. Also, never run
    git init      in your home folder or on your Desktop: only inside a project folder.

The three stages

This is the most important idea in Git. Every change passes through three places:

Staging area                           Repository
 Working directory                                                                       The  .git  folder
 Your folder — you            git add               The “index” —                            — saved
   edit files here                                 what goes in the     git commit          snapshots
                                                     next commit
   menu.txt ✎

menu.txt ✓                              6cb774b
                                                                                           “Add menu”

   📮 Desk → envelope → posted letter. You write on the desk, choose what goes in the envelope,
                                               then post it.

1. Working directory: the files you see and edit.

2. Staging area (also called the index): the changes you have chosen for the next
   snapshot.
3. Repository: the snapshots (commits) saved permanently in                   .git  .

🧠The post office

   You write letters at your desk (working directory). You put the ones that are ready
   into an envelope (staging area); you don't have to send every letter you wrote.
   When you post the envelope (commit), it is sent and recorded.

Why have a staging area at all? Because real work is messy. You may fix a bug and
start a new feature in the same hour. Staging lets you commit them as two clean,
separate commits.

Checking where things are:                 git status

git status      is the command you will type most often. Run it before and after
everything.

          Git Bash

  $ echo "Samosa 15" > menu.txt
  $ git status
  On branch main

  No commits yet

  Untracked files:
    (use "git add <file>--." to include in what will be committed)
            menu.txt

  nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

Untracked means Git sees the file but has never saved it. Notice that Git even tells you
what to do next.

What status says                          Meaning                                     Colour in Git
                                                                                        Bash

  Untracked files                           new file Git has never saved                red

  Changes not staged for commit             a saved file was edited, but not            red
                                            staged

Changes to be committed                   staged, ready for the next commit           green

  nothing to commit, working tree           everything is saved                         n/a
  clean

There is also a short format:       git status -s        prints  ??   for untracked,     M   for
modified (left column = staged, right column = not staged).

Staging changes:            git add

           Git Bash

  $ git add menu.txt
  $ git status
  On branch main

  No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
    (use "git rm --cached <file>--." to unstage)
             new file:   menu.txt

Ways to stage:

  Command                                     Stages

   git add menu.txt                           one file

   git add menu.txt cart.js                   several files

   git add *.css                              every   .css   file in this folder

   git add .                                  everything changed in this folder and below

Staged something by mistake? Unstage it, and your edit stays safe in the file:

          Git Bash

  $ git add .
  $ git restore --staged menu.css
  $ git status -s
  M  menu.txt
  -? menu.css

Saving a snapshot:            git commit

          Git Bash

  $ git commit -m "Add menu"
  [main (root-commit) 6cb774b] Add menu
   1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
   create mode 100644 menu.txt

Read that output: on branch main, the very first (root) commit, its short ID 6cb774b,
your message, and what changed. Every commit gets a unique 40-character ID (a
SHA-1 hash). Git usually shows the first seven characters.

          Git Bash

  $ git log
  commit 6cb774b24074eb78d807a9a2420e109ab07b3a89 (HEAD -> main)
  Author: Krish Patel <krish@example.com>
  Date:   Thu Oct 22 22:55:39 2026 +0530

      Add menu

Krish edits the menu and adds a stylesheet. He commits them separately, because
they are two different changes:
Git Bash

$ echo "Vada Pav 20" -> menu.txt
  $ git diff
  diff --git a/menu.txt b/menu.txt
  index 4b00757-.b0be448 100644
  --- a/menu.txt
  --+ b/menu.txt
  @@ -1 +1,2 @@
   Samosa 15
  +Vada Pav 20
  $ git add menu.txt
  $ git commit -m "Add vada pav to menu"
  [main b0d4373] Add vada pav to menu
   1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
  $ git add menu.css
  $ git commit -m "Add menu styles"
  [main 92bd5b5] Add menu styles
   1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
   create mode 100644 menu.css
  $ git log --onel

ine
  92bd5b5 (HEAD -> main) Add menu styles
  b0d4373 Add vada pav to menu
  6cb774b Add menu

   💡Good commit messages

   Write what the commit does, starting with a verb: "Add vada pav to menu", "Fix
   total when cart is empty". Not "update", "changes" or "final". Your future self,
   and your teammates, read these messages to understand the history.

   📝Shortcut:        git commit -am "message"

-a   stages every modified tracked file before committing. It does not add new
   (untracked) files; those still need     git add    .

Your first repository on GitHub

There are two ways to connect a project to GitHub. Both end in the same place.

Method 1: local first                              Method 2: GitHub
                                                                               first

  Start with                a folder on your computer (   git init   )         a new repo on
                                                                               github.com

  On GitHub, create         empty: don't add a README                          with a README
  the repo…

Then run                   git remote add origin <url>        and  git        git clone <url>
                            push -u origin main

  Best when                 you already have code                              you are starting
                                                                               fresh

To create a repo on GitHub: click + (top right) → New repository → type a name →
choose Public or Private → Create repository. GitHub then shows the exact commands
to run.

⚠"refusing to merge unrelated histories"

   This error appears if you create the GitHub repo with a README and also run                 git
   init   locally, so the two have different first commits. Pick one method. (The fix is
    git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories                   .)

Uploading:        git remote        and    git push

Krish uses Method 1. He created an empty repo on GitHub, so he connects his local
repo to it and pushes:
Git Bash

$ git remote add origin https:-/github.com/krish-patel/amroli-canteen.git
  $ git remote -v
  origin    https:-/github.com/krish-patel/amroli-canteen.git (fetch)
  origin    https:-/github.com/krish-patel/amroli-canteen.git (push)
  $ git push -u origin main
  Enumerating objects: 9, done.
  Counting objects: 100% (9/9), done.
  Writing objects: 100% (9/9), done.
  Total 9 (delta 0), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
  To https:-/github.com/krish-patel/amroli-canteen.git
   * [new branch]

main -> main
  branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.

    origin     is the nickname for the GitHub URL.

    -u   (set upstream) links your      main    to  origin/main     . From now on, plain      git
   push    and   git pull     know where to go.

   📝Signing in

On a real computer the first push opens a browser window from Git Credential
   Manager to sign in to GitHub. GitHub no longer accepts your account password
   typed in the terminal. In this site's Playground the GitHub is simulated, so no sign-
   in is needed.

Downloading a project:               git clone

Hetvi created a repo for project notes. Dhruvi wants a copy on her laptop:

Git Bash

  $ git clone https:-/github.com/hetvi-desai/canteen-docs.git
  Cloning into 'canteen-docs'--.
  remote: Enumerating objects: 3, done.
  remote: Counting objects: 100% (3/3), done.
  remote: Total 3 (delta 0), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
  Receiving objects: 100% (3/3), done.
  $ cd canteen-docs
  $ git remote -v
  origin    https:-/github.com/hetvi-desai/canteen-docs.git (fetch)
  origin    https:-/github.com/hetvi-desai/canteen-docs.git (push)

git clone      downloads every file and the whole history, and sets up               origin     for you.
That's why you don't run        git init     or  git remote add        after cloning.

   ⚠Clone ≠ Download ZIP

   GitHub's Download ZIP button gives you only the files: no history and no
   connection to GitHub. You can't push or pull from it.

Getting your team's work:                git fetch        and    git pull

Overnight, Dhruvi pushed a new file,          orders.py     . Next morning Krish gets her work.

     git fetch                                           git pull

    📦 The parcel arrives at your door.                  📦➡🏠 The parcel is opened and unpacked.

Downloads new commits into                           =  git fetch    + git merge
       origin/main                                         Your branch moves forward
      Your branch and files do not change                  Your files update
      Look first: git log main..origin/main

Look before you leap with         git fetch    :

Git Bash

  $ git fetch
  remote: Enumerating objects: 3, done.
  remote: Counting objects: 100% (3/3), done.
  remote: Total 3 (delta 0), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
  Unpacking objects: 100% (3/3), done.
  From https:-/github.com/krish-patel/amroli-canteen
     92bd5b5-.e423aad  main -> origin/main
  $ git status
  On branch main
  Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 1 commit, and can be fast-forwarded.
    (use "git pull" to update your local branch)

nothing to commit, working tree clean
  $ git log --oneline main-.origin/main
  e423aad (origin/main) Add orders list

Then bring it in with    git pull     (fetch + merge):

          Git Bash

  $ git pull
  Updating 92bd5b5-.e423aad
  Fast-forward
   orders.py | 1 +
   1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
   create mode 100644 orders.py

   ⚠"rejected … (fetch first)"

If a teammate pushed before you, Git refuses your push. Never panic and never
   force it: run  git pull    , then   git push     again.

The daily loop

  ☀   git pull    →      ✏ edit files →      🔍    git status    →      📦   git add    →

  💾   git commit -m     →      ☁   git push

A repository is a folder plus its history in      .git   . git init     creates one.

   Changes move working directory → staging area → repository with                   git add     and
    git commit     .

    git status      tells you where every file is. Read it often.

   Local first:   git remote add origin <url>            then   git push -u origin main          .
   GitHub first:    git clone <url>       .

git fetch      downloads without changing your files;          git pull     downloads and
   merges.

   Commit small, commit often, and write messages that start with a verb.

Practise with Missions M-03 to M-07, then take the Unit 2 quiz.

CHAPTER 3 · UNIT 3 · 6 HOURS
    Branching and Merging

    Work in parallel with branches, bring work together with merges, and calmly resolve conflicts.

      Introduction to branches    Creating & switching branches    Merging & resolving conflicts

      Deleting branches

    Practise online: missions M-08, M-09, M-10, M-11

Why branches?

The Amroli Canteen app works, and Hetvi has shown it to the canteen manager. Now
Krish wants to try a new menu design, and Dhruvi wants to add online payment. Both
changes will take days, and both might break things.

If they edit  main    directly, the working app is broken until they finish. If they don't, they
can't save their progress. Branches solve this.

   🧠Parallel universes

A branch is a parallel universe for your project. Krish can try his new design in his
   own universe. If it works, he brings it back to the main universe (a merge). If it
   fails, he deletes that universe, and       main    never even knew.

With branches:

    main    always stays working, ready to demo.

   Each feature gets its own branch:          feature-menu      ,  feature-payment       .

   Several people work in parallel without disturbing each other.
Finished work is merged back into           main   .

What a branch really is

                                                                         HEAD

                                                                        feature-menu

                                                                D

                                                         main

                  A              B               C

A branch is just a movable label on a commit. HEAD shows which branch you are on. Committing
                                       moves that label forward.

A branch is not a copy of your files. It is a tiny label that points to one commit, which is
why creating a branch is instant.

   When you commit, the current branch's label moves forward to the new commit.

HEAD is a special label that says which branch you are on. Git Bash shows it in the
   prompt:    ~/amroli-canteen (feature-menu)              .

Creating and listing branches

           Git Bash

  $ git branch
  * main
  $ git branch feature-menu
  $ git branch
    feature-menu
  * main

    git branch       lists branches. The     *   marks the one you are on.

    git branch <name>         creates a branch at your current commit, but it does not
   switch to it.

💡Naming branches

$ git switch main

Switching branches changes the files in your folder to match that branch.

Create and switch in one step:

  New way (Git 2.23+)            Classic way                       Does

   git switch <branch>            git checkout <branch>            move to an existing branch
git switch -c <new>            git checkout -b <new>            create a branch and move to it

Both work.    checkout      is older and does many jobs (it also restores files), so newer Git
added the clearer      switch   . You will see    checkout     in many tutorials, so know both.

   ⚠Commit before you switch

   overwritten by checkout". Commit your work (or stash it, Unit 4) first.

Merging: fast-forward

Krish is happy with the new menu. To bring           feature-menu       into  main   , switch to the
branch that receives the changes, then merge:

  $ git switch main

  Updating 8391a89-.b97cb83
  Fast-forward
   menu.txt | 1 +
   1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)

Fast-forward means        main    had no new commits of its own, so Git simply moved the
 main   label forward to Krish's commit. No new commit was needed.

Three-way merges

    Fast-forward                                         Three-way merge

                                         main →

                                                                                              merge

    main had no new commits, so Git just moves           Both branches moved on, so Git joins them
    the label forward. No merge commit.                  with a new merge commit that has two
                                                         parents.

Meanwhile Krish built the cart on         feature-cart       , and someone also added tea to

           Git Bash

$ git merge feature-cart
  Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.

   create mode 100644 cart.js
  $ git log --oneline --graph
  *   de0d069 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'feature-cart'
  |\
  * | 3776e7d Add tea

  * | b97cb83 (feature-menu) Add vada pav to menu
  |/
  * 8391a89 Add opening time
  * 3c16dcc Add menu

Git found the common ancestor (          8391a89     ), combined both sets of changes, and
created a merge commit with two parents. Read the graph from the top: the                      |\   is
where the history splits; the       |/   is where it started.

Merge conflicts

Sometimes Git cannot decide alone. Dhruvi changed the opening time to 8 AM on her
branch; on    main   , Krish changed the same line to 10 AM.

           Git Bash

$ git merge change-timing
  Auto-merging timing.txt
  CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in timing.txt
  Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
  $ git status
  On branch main
  You have unmerged paths.
    (fix conflicts and run "git commit")
    (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge)

  Unmerged paths:
    (use "git add <file>--." to mark resolution)
            both modified:   timing.txt

A conflict happens when two branches change the same lines of the same file. Git
stops and asks a human to decide. That isn't an error: it is Git refusing to guess.

Git writes both versions into the file, between markers:

<<<<<<< HEAD     starts your version (the branch
    <<<<<<< HEAD                                    you are on)
    Open: 10 AM                                      =======    divides the two versions
    =======                                          >>>>>>> change-timing      ends their version (the
    Open: 8 AM                                      branch being merged)
    >>>>>>> change-timing                           To resolve: keep

the right text, delete all three
                                                    marker lines, then  git add    and  git commit

Resolving a conflict, step by step:

1. Open the file (   edit timing.txt        in the Playground, or your editor).

2. Decide the correct content. Keep one side, the other, or a mix.

3. Delete all three marker lines.

4. Mark it resolved:     git add timing.txt        .

5. Finish the merge:      git commit     .

          Git Bash

$ echo "Open: 8 AM" > timing.txt
  $ git add timing.txt
  $ git status
  On branch main
  All conflicts fixed but you are still merging.
    (use "git commit" to conclude merge)

  Changes to be committed:
    (use "git restore --staged <file>--." to unstage)
            modified:   timing.txt
  $ git commit --no-edit
  [main e41ab0c] Merge branch 'change-timing'

   💡The escape hatch

Changed your mind halfway?           git merge --abort         puts everything back exactly
   as it was before the merge.

$ git branch -d experiment

git branch -D <name>                   any branch, even unmerged (its unique commits are

  <name>

Hetvi's four rules for the Amroli Canteen team:

1. Never commit directly to        main   . main    must always work.

2. One feature = one branch:         feature-cart      , fix-total     .

3. Pull before you start, so you branch from the latest           main   .

4. Merge small and often. Small branches mean small conflicts.

$ git switch main

git stash      is like pausing a game and saving it in a slot. Your half-done changes

Git Bash

  Lightweight                  git tag v1.0                  just a name for the commit

Annotated (for               git tag -a v1.1 -m            name + message + who tagged it +
  releases)                   "…"                            date

Undoing changes: which command?
Git has several "undo" commands. Choosing the right one depends on two questions:

Is the change committed?

                         NO                                                  YES

      Edited, not staged →   git restore                           Is it pushed to GitHub?
      <file>
      (classic form:  git checkout --                     Not pushed →     git reset   (--soft / --
      <file>  )                                           mixed / --hard)

Staged by mistake →    git restore --               Pushed →    git revert <commit>
      staged <file>                                       (adds an "undo" commit; safe for the
                                                          team)

   ⚠The golden rule of undo

   Not pushed yet?       reset     is fine: you're only rewriting your own history. Already
   pushed? Use       revert    . It adds a new commit and never rewrites history your
   team already has.

Discarding edits:           git restore         (and     checkout --        )

You edited a file, it's a mess, and you want the last committed version back:

           Git Bash

  $ echo "oops" -> menu.txt
  $ git restore menu.txt
  $ git status -s

The classic command does the same thing:              git checkout -- menu.txt            . (The  --
means "what follows is a file, not a branch".)

⚠No undo for restore

    git restore <file>        permanently throws away the uncommitted edits in that
   file. Git never saved them, so it can't bring them back.

Moving back in time:            git reset

 git reset     moves the current branch back to an earlier commit. The three modes
decide what happens to the changes from the commits you "undo":

    Command                     Moves the             Staging area              Your files
                                branch back

git reset --soft           ✓                     changes stay staged       kept
    HEAD~1

     git reset HEAD~1     (-    ✓                     changes become            kept
    -mixed)                                           unstaged

     git reset --hard           ✓                     cleared                   ⚠ changes
    HEAD~1                                                                      deleted

          Git Bash

$ echo "Dosa 40" -> menu.txt -& git commit -qam "add dosa"
  $ git reset --soft HEAD~1
  $ git status -s
  M  menu.txt
  $ git commit -qm "Add dosa to menu"
  $ git reset HEAD~1
  Unstaged changes after reset:
  M         menu.txt
  $ git commit -qam "Add dosa to menu"
  $ git reset --hard HEAD~1
  HEAD is now at 07f793e Finish cart

    --soft   : perfect for fixing a bad commit message or adding a forgotten file.
   Changes stay staged.

--mixed     (the default): undo the commit and decide again what to stage.

    --hard   : throw the commit and its changes away. ⚠ Use with care.

 git reset <file>        (without a mode) simply unstages a file, like        git restore --
staged   .

Undoing a pushed commit:                 git revert

Krish pushed Finish cart, and it broke the live demo. His teammates have already pulled
it, so rewriting history with   reset    would cause chaos. Instead he reverts it:

          Git Bash

$ git revert HEAD --no-edit
  [main c47f6d3] Revert "Finish cart"
   1 file changed, 1 deletion(-)
  $ git log --oneline -3
  c47f6d3 (HEAD -> main) Revert "Finish cart"
  07f793e (tag: v1.0, tag: v1.1) Finish cart
  26ff36d Fix samosa price

 git revert <commit>         creates a new commit that does the opposite of the old one.
The history stays honest: anyone can see the mistake and its fix. Without              --no-edit    ,
Git opens the editor with a ready-made message.

reset                                revert

  How                       moves the branch back                 adds a new "opposite" commit

  History                   rewritten (commits disappear)         kept (nothing disappears)

  Safe after pushing?       ⚠ No                                  ✅ Yes

Visiting the past: detached HEAD

 git checkout <commit>         lets you look at an old version of the whole project:

Git Bash

  $ git checkout HEAD~2
  Note: switching to 'HEAD~2'.

  You are in 'detached HEAD' state. You can look around, make experimental
  changes and commit them, and you can discard any commits you make in this
  state without impacting any branches by switching back to a branch.
  …
  HEAD is now at 26ff36d Fix samosa price
  $ git switch main
  Switched to branch 'main'

Detached HEAD means HEAD points to a commit instead of a branch. Look around, run
the old code, then     git switch main       to come back. If you want to keep work done
there, create a branch first:    git switch -c old-idea         .

git log     (with  --oneline    ,  --graph --all      , -n  , --author     , --grep   ,  --

Forking: contributing to other projects

You can't push to a repository you don't own. To contribute anyway, you fork it: GitHub
copies it to your account, you change your copy, and you send a pull request back.

                                        "upstream": you can't push here

The seven-step contribution flow:

           Git Bash

$ git clone https:-/github.com/krish-patel/git-practice-2026.git
  $ cd git-practice-2026
  $ git remote add upstream https:-/github.com/sbccas/git-practice-2026.git
  $ git switch -c add-krish-patel
  $ echo "# Krish Patel" > students/krish-patel.md
  $ git add .
  $ git commit -m "Add krish-patel profile card"
  $ git push -u origin add-krish-patel

Then open the pull request from your fork to the original. Later, to get the original's new
commits:     git pull upstream main           , or press Sync fork on your fork's GitHub page.

Open source etiquette

Well-run projects contain a few standard files:

  File                           Purpose

   README.md                     what the project is, how to install and use it

   LICENSE                       what others may legally do with the code

   CONTRIBUTING.md               how to contribute: branch names, code style, PR rules

   .gitignore                    files Git should not track

Before contributing: read        CONTRIBUTING.md        , look for issues labelled good first issue,
keep each PR small and focused, and be polite in reviews.

Unit 5 summary

A repository page shows code, history, branches, issues, pull requests and settings;
   the README is its front page.

   Create repositories with a README (to clone) or empty (to push); choose visibility,
    .gitignore      and licence.

   Issues track bugs and tasks;         fixes #3     in a commit closes issue 3.

   Pull requests propose merging a branch; teammates review, then merge (merge
   commit, squash or rebase).

Fork = your copy on GitHub; contribute with fork → clone → branch → commit →
   push → PR;      upstream     points to the original.
